As someone who has personally spent $500k / mo+ on Google Ads for years, I can tell you with certainty: 

This revenue growth in Search is artificial & extremely unhealthy for Google’s business long term

Search volumes are declining as legacy search is being increasingly cannibalized by non-monetized LLM queries

Google’s response? 

Manufacture revenue growth via short-sighted, highly extractive, customer-hostile tactics. I.e. charge advertisers more for lower quality clicks, including clicks they do not want and explicitly did not approve Google to charge them for

A few examples to illustrate: 

For all of its history until recently, Google operated on a 2nd price auction model

I.e. if you bid $5 CPC and the next highest bidder bids $1 CPC, Google charged you $1.01 for the click (one penny more than the 2nd highest bidder) rather than the $5 you bid

This was a genius move by Google early on as it incentivizes advertisers to input their true maximum willingness to pay rather than trying to play the game of bidding low and constantly adjusting to try to stay just ahead of the next highest bidder while still not paying too much

However recently, Google silently deprecated the 2nd price auction and began charging advertisers as much as their bid and budget caps allow, regardless of what anyone else is bidding

It’s a short-sighted cash grab at the expense of the long term health of the  advertiser ecosystem

A lot of ink has been spilled on GPU financing lately. I spent over a decade trading ABS on Wall St, and structured over $2B+ of debt financings as an operator (including at @tryramp). Figured I'd try to make sense of this market, so I went back to a framework I knew well: aircraft ABS and aircraft engine ABS.

My take: a GPU neocloud runs on airline economics, and the debt behind it looks a lot like aircraft engine ABS.

The parallels:

• Perishable inventory. An empty seat after the door closes is gone forever. So is an idle hour on an energized H100 rack.
• 85%+ of cost is fixed (servers, 10-year rack leases, 10-14% debt service). One more hour of compute costs pennies of power.
• Utilization is everything. Airlines break even around 80% load factor, a levered GPU cluster around 65-75%. The returns live in those last 25 percentage points.
• NVIDIA is Boeing and Airbus rolled into one. Powered shells and grid interconnects are the new airport slots.
• Wall St copied the aircraft financing playbook: take-or-pay contract plus servers in a bankruptcy-remote SPV, 70-80% LTV.

posts.text:
Cliff Sosin on why Jevons paradox taps out and the market for intelligence could shrink:

"Jevons paradox is just a narrow example of price elasticity of demand. In general, all markets are U-shaped.

When the product is terrible, there's no demand. Then the product gets better and people will pay a lot, but they won't buy very much. 

As the price goes down, the size of the market will rise. But then you get to a point where further price decreases don't drive enough demand and the market shrinks. 

If you take the price to zero, the size of the market goes to zero.

One example that I've thought about is the cost of fiber optic communication, or just communication.

The cost of moving information used to be super high and people moved very little of it. Then the cost of moving information went down a lot and the amount of information moved went up a ton. 

Then the market stopped growing and the cost kept falling and the market kept shrinking. 

Cogent Communications, I think, routes 30 or 40% of all IP traffic across the internet. And Cogent Communications is a few billion dollar market cap company. It's just not a very big industry.

I'm not saying that we're going to get quite that small in terms of intelligence, but Jevons paradox is a statement about a particular spot on a curve."

This is a HUGE point for any hedge fund investor and trader (when assessing a return stream). 

I’ve seen this across a few exceptional funds. A strategy might have a historical CAGR of 15% with a maximum drawdown of just 5%. Excellent numbers on paper. But investors don’t all enter on the first day of that track record.

Suppose you invest when the fund is already up 15% for the year. The next four monthly returns are -1%, -1.5%, -1%, and -1.5%.

Your experience is now a roughly 5% loss. You participated in none of the gains that preceded it, but all of the subsequent drawdown.

Almost immediately, regret can set in. You question the allocation, the manager, and the process, even though those losses could reflect ordinary variance within the strategy rather than any deterioration in its edge. It’s a psychological phenomenon that overtakes even some experienced investors. It’s never a good feeling to see losses when you deploy capital towards a strategy. 

But this is something that’s important to distinguish early on and that only comes from truly understanding the process and potential distribution. If you don’t, you’ll just end up becoming a return chaser that crab trades / invests their way into suboptimal returns. 

Process before everything and the rest will take care of itself.

posts.name: The Kobeissi Letter
posts.text:
Demand is becoming a bigger driver of US inflation:

Demand-driven components contributed +1.2 percentage points to the +3.4% YoY increase in PCE inflation in August, the largest contribution since September 2023.

At the same time, supply-driven factors added +1.0 percentage point, while ambiguous factors accounted for another +1.2 percentage points.

This contrasts with the post-pandemic inflation surge, when supply disruptions were the main driver.

In 2022, supply-driven components contributed an average of +3.1 percentage points per month to headline PCE inflation, compared with +2.6 percentage points per month from demand-driven factors.

This is a key distinction for Fed policy, as rising interest rates can slow demand, while their impact on supply-side pressures is limited.

The composition of US inflation is shifting.
